content: Blocking an enzyme’s production restored brain growth and healthy behaviors in mice engineered to develop Angelman syndrome, pointing to a possible treatment target. Children with Angelman syndrome begin to show difficulties with thinking and movement at around 6 months of age. The rare condition occurs in approximately one in 20,000 births and is caused by the absence of a gene normally inherited from the mother. Researchers know which gene is missing, but they have struggled to explain why its absence causes these problems, making treatments elusive. Research in mice now points to a chain of events that connects the missing gene to a stress response that interferes with brain growth. A team led by Jason Yi, PhD, an assistant professor of neuroscience at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis , traced that response to a buildup of a normally harmless enzyme. The study was published in Nature . The missing gene, UBE3A , produces an enzyme called ubiquitin ligase, which helps keep cells orderly by marking unneeded proteins for disposal. It is active throughout the brain and participates in 60 different cellular processes. Identifying which of those processes contribute to Angelman syndrome required narrowing that broad field of possibilities. Yi and his colleagues developed modified cells in the laboratory with UBE3A deactivated, then looked for proteins that accumulated without it. They identified 23 candidate proteins whose levels increased. One stood out for its strong connection to ubiquitin ligase’s normal housekeeping function: asparagine synthetase, an enzyme that helps cells produce essential proteins. In mice genetically modified to develop Angelman syndrome, elevated levels of asparagine synthetase activated the brain’s stress response. Yet the enzyme does not interact with the usual triggers for that response, and its overabundance does not otherwise damage the cell. The consequences instead arise indirectly, as the stress response sharply reduces protein production and growth. “The neurons are tricked into thinking that they’re in stress when they’re not — that’s bad because they will then not grow normally,” Yi said, noting that most children with Angelman syndrome have smaller brains than their peers of the same age. “It’s a reaction from the brain trying to conserve resources to protect itself. It does suggest that there is a dysregulation in the brain we might be able to correct.” Blocking the production of asparagine synthetase restored normal brain growth and healthy behaviors in the mice. The team had corrected a later step in the biological sequence set off by the missing gene, allowing healthy development to resume. The study is the first to link an increase in asparagine synthetase to a neurological condition. It adds to evidence that an imbalance in proteins can contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders by triggering stress responses, even when the proteins themselves are not directly damaging cells. Yi said medications could potentially target the stress response triggered by asparagine synthetase, but much remains to be learned before work on a possible treatment can begin. His team is investigating precisely why the enzyme activates that response, where in the brain the response is most active, and when during development medical interventions would be most effective. “We still don’t know a whole lot about the disease,” said Yi. “We haven’t been able to identify all of the things that the missing gene is doing and rescue the things that it is not doing in Angelman’s syndrome. But I think our data are the most complete so far to begin answering those questions.” Reference: “Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes” by Kwang-Soo Kim, Cory Gardner, Alissa Cullen, Jalin A. Stelzer, Kevin Cho, Ashish Sharma, Mati T. Nemera, Travis Law, Huma Naz, Guoyan Zhao, Harrison W. Gabel, Gary J. Patti, Erik S. Musiek, Tae-Hyuk Ahn and Jason J. Yi, 21 October 2026, Nature . DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11165-4 Support for this work came from the Simons Foundation (Bridge to Independence award #387973), the Whitehall Foundation, the Hope Center for Neurological Disorders at Washington University (Pilot Award), and the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH122786 and R01MH144153). Switching from a vegetarian to a vegan diet altered liver metabolism in mice within just two days, making glucose production and toxic waste removal less efficient. Millions of people follow a vegan diet, excluding all animal-derived products. Plant-based eating is recommended in part for its environmental benefits, but the health consequences of getting all dietary protein from plants are not yet fully understood. For researchers, that raises a question about how the body responds when the source of its protein changes. Scientists at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) investigated that question in mice, focusing on the liver, which helps maintain blood sugar and processes the components of dietary protein. Their study, published in Molecu l ar Metabolism , compared a lacto-vegetarian diet containing both animal and plant proteins with a vegan diet. “In just two days, the mice fed an exclusively vegan diet showed less efficient glucose production,” explains Pierre Maechler, full professor in the Department of Cell Physiology and Metabolism and at the Diabetes Center of the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine. “Furthermore, their livers were less effective at eliminating ammonia, a toxic substance released during the breakdown of amino acids. A significant reduction in physical activity also suggests effects on the body as a whole.” Proteins from plants and animals consist of amino acids, small molecules joined together like links in a chain. Their types and proportions differ depending on the food source, so changing protein sources gives the body a different mixture to process. Plant proteins naturally contain fewer branched-chain amino acids than animal proteins. Along with helping build the body’s proteins, these amino acids supply some of the raw material the liver uses to produce glucose and maintain sufficient blood sugar during fasting. “Overall, a change in diet alters liver metabolism very quickly, but this effect is just as rapidly reversible,” emphasizes Maechler. “The body adapts within one to two days to even subtle changes in dietary composition and returns to normal upon the reintroduction of animal proteins.” The combination of less efficient glucose production and ammonia removal pointed the team toward a liver enzyme called glutamate dehydrogenase, or GDH. Located in mitochondria, the structures inside cells that help process fuel, GDH connects protein metabolism with sugar metabolism. To investigate its role, the researchers compared two groups of mice lacking the enzyme in their livers. One group ate a lacto-vegetarian diet, while the other ate a strict vegan diet. Without GDH, the mice eating only plant proteins developed a severe buildup of ammonia and impaired blood glucose regulation compared with mice whose diet also included animal proteins. This confirmed the enzyme’s essential role in the metabolic response to an exclusively plant-based diet. The experiments were conducted in mice, so they do not establish that people would experience the same changes. They do, however, provide a way to investigate the physiological questions that accompany a change in protein source. “In addition to the ethical and environmental considerations that often motivate a switch to a plant-based diet, there are also scientific factors relating to the physiological functioning of our metabolism that are worth being aware of,” notes Maechler. For people following a strict vegan diet, the researchers emphasize choosing protein sources rich in branched-chain amino acids, such as nuts, tofu, and lentils, to support the liver’s metabolic functions. They place that consideration alongside the need to ensure an adequate intake of specific vitamins. Reference: “Transition to dietary plant-based proteins requires functional liver GDH for proper control of ammonia and energy homeostasis” by Yan Zhou, Angela M. Ramos-Lobo, Tingting Fu, Hector Gallart-Ayala, Julijana Ivanisevic and Pierre Maechler, 4 September 2026, Molecular Metabolism . DOI: 10.1016/j.molmet.2026.102435 The work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (#310030_192486 to P.M.) and the canton of Geneva.
